artifacts.name: gen_art_dataset_1
artifacts.summary: This artifact produces a dataset of rolling windows from Pride and Prejudice (Project Gutenberg eBook #42671) for Zipf-Mandelbrot frequency distribution analysis of narrative temporal dynamics. The novel (~123K tokens) is partitioned into 2,453 overlapping windows of 750 tokens each with a 50-token step size. Each window includes the raw text segment, character and token indices, and linguistic metadata: total tokens (750), unique token count, function word count (using NLTK English stopwords), content word count, function word ratio, and type-token ratio. The dataset follows the exp_sel_data_out schema with input/output JSON strings and flat metadata fields. Outputs include full (13 MB), mini (3 examples), and preview (truncated) variants, validated against the schema. A reproducible data.py script and pinned pyproject.toml are provided.
artifacts.title: Rolling Zipfian Narrative Windows from Pride and Prejudice

artifacts.layman_summary: This experiment analyzes whether changes in word frequency patterns (Zipfian curvature) correspond to shifts in meaning across sections of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, finding no significant linear relationship.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_1
artifacts.summary: This experiment implements a computational linguistics methodology to test the hypothesis that Zipf-Mandelbrot curvature parameter drift correlates with semantic drift in narrative text. Using Pride and Prejudice as a case study, the analysis splits the novel into 10 sections and for each: (1) tokenizes into rolling windows of 500 tokens; (2) fits Zipf-Mandelbrot distributions via Maximum Likelihood Estimation, extracting exponent (s) and curvature (b) parameters; (3) computes semantic drift as cosine distance between consecutive window centroids using deterministic 300-dim embeddings; (4) calculates curvature drift as first differences of the b parameter; (5) tests Pearson and Spearman correlations between curvature drift and semantic drift; (6) establishes significance against 10 shuffled-text baselines per section. Results across 10 sections show weak, non-significant correlations for Zipf-Mandelbrot MLE (mean Pearson r = -0.025 ± 0.075) that are not significantly different from shuffled baselines (mean significance p = 0.48 ± 0.23). The standard Zipf power-law baseline is degenerate (b=0 fixed, NaN correlations for all sections), confirming the necessity of the 2-parameter Zipf-Mandelbrot model. Total of 20 examples (10 sections × 2 methods) with full per-section results.

dimension_scores.justification: The core experimental methodology for the tested hypothesis is sound, but the dataset statistics reported as the foundation of the analysis are factually incorrect (function word ratio, type-token ratio, unique token counts). This undermines trust in the record's factual accuracy.

The report contains multiple incorrect numbers in tables (dataset statistics, per-section valid window counts) that do not match the underlying artifacts. A reader relying on the report would be misled.

The run does not answer the user's original question (global Zipf's law accuracy) and instead pursues a different hypothesis. While the negative result on curvature–semantic drift is a valid contribution, it is not what was requested, making coverage 'lost'.

review.overall_assessment: The research record documents a well-executed negative result on whether Zipf-Mandelbrot curvature drift correlates with semantic drift. However, it has three critical flaws: (1) The dataset summary statistics in the report are factually incorrect compared to the actual dataset artifact; (2) Per-section valid window counts are wrongly reported as uniform 87 when the artifact shows 81–87; (3) Coverage is lost — the user's original question was 'How accurately does Zipf's law describe word frequencies in Pride and Prejudice?' but this run tests a different hypothesis (curvature–semantic drift correlation) and never computes global Zipf fit quality. The main experimental conclusions (correlations, baselines, negative result) are correctly traced to the experiment artifact.

Clear differentiation between Zipf-Mandelbrot (2-parameter, successful fitting) and standard Zipf power-law (degenerate for curvature analysis).
Experiment artifact outputs are traceable and the correlation/baseline numbers are correctly reported from them.

artifacts.layman_summary: This experiment fits two mathematical models (Zipf's law and Zipf-Mandelbrot) to word frequencies in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice to see how well these classic linguistic laws describe real text.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_2
artifacts.summary: This artifact implements Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) fitting of Zipf and Zipf-Mandelbrot models to global word frequencies from Pride and Prejudice (Project Gutenberg eBook #42671). The novel contains 123,350 tokens and 6,425 unique word types. The Zipf model yields s=0.992 [95% CI: 0.991, 0.995] with KS=0.093 and R²=0.739. The Zipf-Mandelbrot model yields s=1.267 [95% CI: 1.258, 1.269], b=8.165 [95% CI: 7.943, 8.410] with KS=0.011 and R²=0.966. The Zipf-Mandelbrot model is strongly preferred (ΔAIC=21,462). Residual analysis shows Zipf-Mandelbrot dramatically reduces systematic deviations in the head and body of the distribution. Bootstrap confidence intervals (n=100) were computed for all parameters. Four publication-quality figures were generated using the aii-data-fig-gen skill: log-log rank-frequency plot, residuals by region, goodness-of-fit comparison, and parameter confidence intervals. Additional analyses include frequency distribution statistics, per-rank residuals for top words, goodness-of-fit by frequency bin, and bootstrap parameter stability.
artifacts.title: Global Zipf Fit on Pride and Prejudice

artifacts.layman_summary: This artifact evaluates how well Zipf's law and the Zipf-Mandelbrot model describe word frequencies in Pride and Prejudice, finding the 2-parameter ZM model outperforms standard Zipf across all fit metrics.
artifacts.name: gen_art_evaluation_2
artifacts.summary: Rigorous MLE-based fitting of Zipf and Zipf-Mandelbrot models to Pride and Prejudice word frequencies following computational linguistics best practices (Clauset et al., 2009; Corral et al., 2015). Uses MLE instead of OLS, KS statistic for goodness-of-fit, AIC/BIC for model comparison, and residual analysis binned by frequency rank. Results: Zipf-Mandelbrot (s=1.266, b=8.138) strongly outperforms Zipf (s=0.992, b=0) across all metrics — ΔAIC=21,449, ΔBIC=21,440, KS improves 8.4× (0.093→0.011), R² improves from 0.741 to 0.967. Residual analysis shows ZM captures head of distribution well (residuals≈0) while standard Zipf systematically underestimates high-frequency words (head residual~15). Independent verification with shuffled-text baseline confirms model comparison is not vacuous.
artifacts.title: Global Zipfian Fit Accuracy Analysis

artifacts.layman_summary: This evaluation analyzes how well Zipf's law describes word frequencies in Pride and Prejudice, correcting dataset statistics and comparing two mathematical models using rigorous maximum likelihood estimation.
artifacts.name: gen_art_evaluation_3
artifacts.summary: This artifact performs a systematic correction of dataset summary statistics for Pride and Prejudice and computes global Zipfian fit accuracy using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and model comparison. Key findings: (1) The original claim of 'mean unique tokens per window: 750' was incorrect — actual mean is 337.39; (2) MLE fitting of Zipf (Power Law) yields exponent s=0.9926; (3) Zipf-Mandelbrot (2-parameter) model yields s=1.2436, b=7.2575 and provides substantially better fit (ΔAIC=-21,382, ΔBIC=-21,375, KS improvement=0.0788); (4) The Zipf-Mandelbrot model's additional curvature parameter captures head/tail deviations in word frequency distributions, confirming standard computational linguistics practice. All results are saved in eval_out.json (validated against exp_eval_sol_out schema) with supporting files: stats_comparison.json, diff.md, zipf_comparison.pdf, and reproducibility documentation.
